options.why: That is afterload.

options.t: The resistance to flow in systemic vessels
options.why: That is systemic vascular resistance.

options.t: The percentage of blood ejected per beat
options.why: That is ejection fraction.

questions.stem: What is afterload?
questions.why: Afterload is the force the ventricles must contract against in order to eject blood. Stroke volume is influenced by preload, afterload, and the contractile state of the myocardium.

options.why: That is end-systolic volume.

options.t: The force the ventricles contract against
The volume of blood returning to the heart
options.why: That is preload.

options.t: The rate at which the ventricles contract
options.why: That is heart rate.

questions.stem: What does Starling's law state?
questions.why: Starling's law states that cardiac muscle, when stretched, contracts with greater force. Increasing preload stretches the muscle, which is one way the heart increases stroke volume.

options.t: Oxygen demand tracks the heart rate
options.why: That relates demand to workload.

options.t: Blood flows from higher to lower pressure
options.why: That is a general principle of flow.

options.t: Output falls as heart rate climbs higher
options.why: That describes a limitation at high rates, not Starling's law.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an inotropic and a chronotropic effect?
questions.why: Inotropic refers to contractility, chronotropic to rate. Chrono is time — an easy hook for remembering which is which, and both terms describe drug effects you will use.

options.why: Both terms apply to the heart as a whole.

options.t: Inotropic is force; chronotropic is rate
Inotropic is rate; chronotropic is force
options.why: The two are reversed here.
Neither term refers to loading conditions.

questions.stem: Blood pressure is a function of which two variables?
questions.why: Blood pressure is a function of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance. SVR is the resistance to blood flow in all vessels except the pulmonary vessels.

options.why: Those determine cardiac output.
Those determine stroke volume.
Those describe output, not pressure.

questions.stem: Resistance to the flow of blood is determined by what?
questions.why: Resistance to blood flow is determined by vessel diameter and the tone of the vascular musculature — which is why vasoconstriction and vasodilation change blood pressure so directly.

options.t: The viscosity of the blood alone
options.why: Viscosity contributes but calibre and tone are the determinants.

options.t: The number of circulating red cells
options.why: Cell count affects viscosity indirectly.

options.t: The heart rate and stroke volume
options.why: Those determine output rather than resistance.

questions.stem: The left coronary artery divides into which two branches, and what do they supply?
questions.why: The left coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending and the circumflex coronary artery, both branching widely to supply the left ventricle, the interventricular septum, and part of the right ventricle.

options.t: The circumflex and marginal, feeding the right
options.why: The marginal branch is a right coronary branch.

options.t: The LAD and circumflex, feeding the left side
The anterior and posterior descending arteries
options.why: The posterior descending arises from the right side.

options.t: The septal and diagonal, feeding conduction
options.why: Those are smaller branches of the LAD.

questions.stem: The right coronary artery supplies which structures?
questions.why: The right coronary artery travels between the right atrium and ventricle by way of the atrioventricular groove. Its branches supply the right atrium and ventricle, part of the inferior left ventricle, and portions of the conduction system.

options.t: The pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch
options.why: Those are great vessels, not coronary territory.

options.t: The right atrium and right ventricle only
options.why: It also supplies part of the inferior left ventricle.

options.t: The whole left ventricle and the septum
options.why: That is the left coronary artery's territory.

questions.stem: What is collateral circulation?
questions.why: Numerous connections — anastomoses — between arterioles of the various coronary arteries allow alternative routes of blood flow. Collateral circulation is the formation of those additional connecting vessels.

options.t: Blood shunted from the periphery during shock
options.why: That is shunting during shock.

options.t: Blood circulating through the lung capillaries
options.why: That is pulmonary circulation.

options.t: Backflow of venous blood to the coronary sinus
options.why: That is coronary sinus drainage.

questions.stem: Which property describes the ability of cardiac pacemaker cells to create an electrical impulse without being stimulated from another source?
questions.why: Automaticity is the ability to generate an impulse independently. Excitability is responding to a stimulus, conductivity is passing an impulse along, and contractility is shortening in response.

options.why: That is passing an impulse onward.
That is shortening in response.
That is responding to a stimulus.

questions.stem: Which property enables a cardiac cell to receive an electrical impulse and pass it on to an adjoining cell?
questions.why: Conductivity enables a cardiac cell to receive an impulse and pass it to the next cell. Contractility is the ability of myocardial cells to shorten in response to that impulse.

options.why: That is shortening in response.
That is responding to a stimulus.
That is generating an impulse independently.

questions.stem: What are the components of the conduction system, in order?
questions.why: Sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, right and left bundle branches, then Purkinje fibers. The SA node is the site of origin of the electrical impulse.

options.t: Purkinje, branches, His, AV node, SA node
options.why: That reverses the sequence entirely.

options.t: SA node, His, AV node, Purkinje, branches
options.why: The AV node comes before the bundle of His.

options.t: AV node, SA node, Purkinje, His, branches
options.why: The SA node fires before the AV node.

options.t: SA node, AV node, His, branches, Purkinje

questions.stem: Which structure is the site of origin of the heart's electrical impulse?
questions.why: The SA node is the site of origin of the electrical impulse — the heart's natural pacemaker.

options.why: That relays the impulse onward from the atria.
Those distribute the impulse through the ventricles.
That carries the impulse into the septum.

questions.stem: In general, cardiac cells have which two types of function?
questions.why: Cardiac cells have either a mechanical (contractile) function or an electrical (pacemaker) function. The electrical stimuli control the mechanical pumping action.

options.why: Those describe nerve fibers.
Those describe neurotransmitter effects.
Those describe metabolic pathways.

questions.stem: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart?
questions.why: Branches of the vagus nerves provide parasympathetic innervation. The ANS innervates the heart by means of cardiac nerves, with sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers forming cardiac plexuses.

options.why: That supplies the diaphragm.
Those supply the chest wall.
That supplies the neck muscles.

questions.stem: Where do the fibers of the cardiac plexuses terminate?
questions.why: The cardiac plexus fibers course along the base of the heart, distribute to the various chambers, penetrate the myocardium, and terminate in the SA node, AV node, atrial myocardium, and ventricles.

options.why: They reach the atria and nodes as well.
They terminate in conducting and muscle tissue.

options.t: SA node, AV node, atria, and ventricles
The sinoatrial node and nowhere else
options.why: They also reach the AV node and myocardium.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as a factor influencing heart rate?
questions.why: Factors influencing heart rate include sympathetic (accelerator) nerve stimulation, electrolyte and hormone levels, metabolic rate, medications, stress, anxiety, fear, and body temperature.

options.why: Cell count is not a listed rate factor.
Viscosity affects resistance rather than rate.
Lung capacity is a respiratory measure.

questions.stem: What are the three layers of a blood vessel wall, from inner to outer?
questions.why: The smooth thin inner lining is the tunica intima or endothelium; the middle layer is the tunica media of elastic tissue and smooth muscle; the outer layer of elastic and collagenous fibers is the tunica adventitia.

options.why: Those are the heart wall layers.
That reverses the order.
Intima is innermost, not second.

questions.stem: When baroreceptors in the central circulation detect a drop in pressure, what happens?
questions.why: The total volume of all vessels forms a large dynamic container. If baroreceptors detect a pressure drop, the vessels constrict to shrink that container proportionally.

options.why: Dilation would worsen the pressure drop.

options.t: The heart slows to conserve oxygen use
options.why: Rate usually rises rather than falls.

options.t: Blood shifts from organs to the periphery
options.why: Blood is directed toward organs, not away.

questions.stem: What is shunting, and what is it a hallmark sign of?
questions.why: In shunting the autonomic nervous system changes blood distribution by constricting peripheral vessels to a greater degree than those supplying the vital organs. This is a hallmark sign of shock.

options.t: Blood pools in the veins during heart failure
options.why: That is venous congestion.

options.t: Blood bypasses the lungs to reach the body
options.why: That is a right-to-left cardiac shunt.

options.t: Blood crosses between atria through a defect
options.why: That is a septal defect.

options.t: Periphery clamps down to protect organs — shock

questions.stem: What are the three main regions of the aorta?
questions.why: Ascending aorta, aortic arch, and descending aorta. The ascending aorta originates at the base of the heart and terminates by becoming the arch; the descending aorta is named according to its location within the body cavities.

options.t: The ascending aorta, the thoracic aorta, and the abdominal aorta
options.why: Thoracic and abdominal are subdivisions of the descending aorta.

options.t: The ascending aorta, the aortic arch, and the descending aorta
The aortic root, the aortic arch, and the aortic bifurcation
options.why: Root and bifurcation are points, not regions.

options.t: The proximal, middle, and distal aorta
options.why: Those are not the named anatomical regions.

questions.stem: Arterioles are described as which type of vessel, and what is their action compared to?
questions.why: Arterioles are the resistance vessels. Their strong muscular walls act as stopcocks through which blood is released into the capillaries.

options.why: Those are the venules and veins.
Those are the capillaries.
Those are the large arteries.

questions.stem: What distinguishes conducting arteries from distributing arteries?
questions.why: Conducting arteries are the large vessels arising from the aorta and its main branches, transporting blood under high pressure. Distributing (muscular) arteries supply individual organs and carry larger amounts of smooth muscle, giving the body the ability to adjust blood flow.

options.t: Conducting have more muscle; distributing elastic
options.why: Distributing arteries carry more smooth muscle.

options.t: Conducting are large; distributing have muscle
Conducting serve limbs; distributing the trunk
options.why: Both types occur throughout the body.

options.t: Conducting supply organs; distributing are large
options.why: The two are reversed here.

questions.stem: The brachiocephalic artery divides into which two vessels?
questions.why: The brachiocephalic artery divides into the right common carotid and the right subclavian artery. Each common carotid then branches at the mandible into the internal and external carotids — the carotid bifurcation.

options.t: The internal and external carotid arteries
options.why: That division happens higher, at the carotid bifurcation.

options.t: Right common carotid and right subclavian
The right subclavian and right axillary
options.why: The axillary comes after the subclavian, not from it.

options.t: The left and right common carotid arteries
options.why: The left common carotid arises separately from the arch.

questions.stem: The subclavian artery becomes which vessel at the shoulder joint, and which below the head of the humerus?
questions.why: At the shoulder joint the subclavian becomes the axillary artery, then the brachial artery below the head of the humerus.

options.t: The radial artery, then the ulnar artery
options.why: Those branch from the brachial artery lower down.

options.t: The brachial artery, then the axillary artery
options.why: The axillary comes before the brachial.

options.t: The axillary artery, then the brachial artery
The carotid artery, then the vertebral artery
options.why: The carotid supplies the head, not the arm.

questions.stem: What are the three major unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta's visceral arteries?
questions.why: The three major unpaired branches are the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric, and the inferior mesenteric arteries.

options.why: Those are terminal branches of the aorta.
Those are paired branches.
Those branch from the celiac trunk.

questions.stem: The femoral artery becomes which vessel in the lower thigh, and what does that branch into?
questions.why: The femoral becomes the popliteal artery in the lower thigh, which branches into the anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries. At the foot the anterior tibial becomes the dorsalis pedis.

options.t: External iliac, then tibial and dorsalis pedis
options.why: The external iliac becomes the femoral, upstream of this.

options.t: Dorsalis pedis, then the plantar arteries
options.why: That is a terminal branch at the foot.

options.t: Popliteal, then the tibial and peroneal
Internal iliac, then peroneal and plantar
options.why: The internal iliac supplies the pelvis.

questions.stem: Venules are called capacitance vessels. What proportion of the body's blood does the venous system contain?
questions.why: The venous system contains 70% of the body's blood, which is why venules are called capacitance or storage vessels. Veins adjust the blood volume returning to the heart — preload — to meet the body's needs.

options.why: That understates venous capacity.
That overstates it, leaving too little elsewhere.
That greatly understates venous capacity.

questions.stem: The external and internal jugular veins join which vessels, and what do those form?
questions.why: External and internal jugular veins join the subclavian veins to form the brachiocephalic veins, which drain into the superior vena cava. Venous sinuses are the primary means of venous drainage from the brain into the internal jugular.

options.why: There is no carotid vein by that name.
That drains the thoracic wall.
Those drain the upper limb.

questions.stem: Which is the longest vein in the body, and what does it drain?
questions.why: The great saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body, draining the foot, leg, and thigh. It originates over the dorsal and medial side of the foot and empties into the femoral vein.

options.t: Basilic vein — the arm and the shoulder
options.why: That drains the upper limb.

options.t: Great saphenous — foot, leg, and thigh
Femoral vein — the thigh and the pelvis
options.why: That is shorter and drains into the iliac.

options.t: Inferior vena cava — the entire lower body
options.why: That is the largest vein but not the longest.

questions.stem: Which organs' venous blood enters the hepatic portal system before reaching the inferior vena cava?
questions.why: Venous blood from the gallbladder, intestines, pancreas, spleen, and stomach first enters the hepatic portal system, passing through the liver before reaching the inferior vena cava. Blood from most other abdominal organs returns directly to the IVC.

options.why: Those are not abdominal digestive organs.
Those drain to the iliac veins.
Those drain directly into the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: What is distinctive about how blood returns from the digestive tract to the heart?
questions.why: Blood from the digestive tract passes through two sets of capillaries before returning to the heart — once in the abdominal organs and again in the liver, where nutrients are extracted and stored.

options.t: It crosses two capillary beds en route
It enters the left atrium instead of right
options.why: All venous return enters the right atrium.

options.t: It bypasses the inferior vena cava entirely
options.why: It reaches the vena cava after passing the liver.

options.t: It returns through lymph rather than veins
options.why: Nutrients travel by portal vein, not lymph.

questions.stem: Which vessels make up the microcirculation?
questions.why: The microcirculation is the portion of the vasculature consisting of arterioles, capillaries, and venules. Its most important functions are transport of nutrients to the tissues and removal of cellular waste.

options.t: The aorta, its main branches, and the venae cavae
options.why: Those are the largest vessels in the body.
Veins are too large to belong to it.
Arteries are too large to belong to the microcirculation.

questions.stem: What do capillaries allow to be exchanged between the blood and the interstitial fluid?
questions.why: Capillaries form the connection between arterioles and venules and allow exchange of gases, water, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones, and waste products between the blood and interstitial fluid.

options.why: Capillaries exchange far more than the gases.
Nutrients and hormones cross as well.
Gases and water cross as well.

questions.stem: What is the difference between hydrostatic and oncotic pressure in the capillary?
questions.why: Hydrostatic pressure is exerted by a liquid and occurs when blood moves through the artery at relatively high pressures — pushing outward. Oncotic pressure is a form of osmotic pressure exerted by plasma proteins that tends to pull water back into the circulatory system.

options.t: Hydrostatic pushes out; oncotic pulls in

options.why: Both act across the capillary bed.

options.t: Both push fluid out at differing rates
options.why: Oncotic pressure pulls fluid inward.

options.t: Hydrostatic pulls in; oncotic pushes out
options.why: The two are reversed here.

questions.stem: Match each heart valve to the structures it separates.
questions.why: Two AV valves and two semilunar valves. The AV valves have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles; the semilunar valves work on pressure alone.
pairs: Right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk

questions.stem: Match each property of cardiac cells to its definition.
questions.why: Four properties that let the heart run itself. Automaticity is the one unique to cardiac tissue — no other muscle generates its own impulse.
pairs: Creating an electrical impulse without stimulation from another source
Receiving an impulse and passing it to an adjoining cell
Shortening in response to an impulse, resulting in contraction

questions.stem: Match each cardiac term to its definition.
questions.why: Output is per minute, stroke volume is per beat, ejection fraction is a percentage. Preload is what comes in, afterload is what it has to push against.
pairs: The amount of blood pumped by the ventricles in one minute
The amount of blood ejected per contraction
The percentage of blood leaving the heart with each contraction
Volume in the ventricle at end of diastole; reflects venous return
The force the ventricles must contract against to eject blood
An effect on the contractility of muscle tissue

questions.stem: On the diagram, blood passing through the tricuspid valve flows next into which chamber?
questions.why: The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle — blood crosses it into the right ventricle before being pumped to the lungs.

options.why: The left ventricle receives blood through the mitral valve.
The right atrium is where that blood just came from.
The pulmonary artery comes after the pulmonic valve, one step later.

questions.stem: Which labeled valve on the diagram controls flow out of the left ventricle?
questions.why: Left ventricular output passes the aortic valve into the ascending aorta; the mitral valve guards the inflow from the left atrium.

options.why: The pulmonary valve is the right ventricle's outflow.
The tricuspid sits on the right side of the heart.
The mitral valve controls flow INTO the left ventricle.

questions.stem: Which labeled structure on this conduction diagram is the heart's primary pacemaker?
questions.why: The sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall initiates each beat; the impulse then travels to the AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers.

options.why: The bundle of His carries it into the septum afterward.
The AV node relays and delays the impulse.
Purkinje fibers are the final distribution network.

questions.stem: On the diagram, an impulse leaving the AV node travels next through which labeled structure?
questions.why: The conduction sequence: SA node → internodal pathways → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.

options.why: Purkinje fibers come last, after the bundle branches.
Bachmann's bundle carries atrial conduction, before the AV node.
The SA node is upstream — the impulse started there.
